courses.title: Computed Tomography and Magnetic Resonance Imaging
courses.description: Principles and technology of CT and MRI, image reconstruction and artefacts, contrast agents, protocols, and safety.

topics.title: CT Principles and Technology
topics.summary: Generations of CT, helical and multislice scanning, Hounsfield units and scan parameters.

material.heading: History and hardware
material.body: Computed tomography was invented by Godfrey Hounsfield (with Allan Cormack's mathematical work; Nobel Prize 1979). A CT scanner rotates an X-ray tube and opposing detector array around the patient in the gantry, measuring attenuation from many angles; a computer reconstructs cross-sectional images. Modern scanners are third-generation designs (rotate–rotate) using slip-ring technology for continuous rotation, enabling helical (spiral) scanning in which the table moves continuously; multidetector (multislice) CT acquires many slices per rotation (64-slice and beyond), permitting thin-section volumetric imaging, CT angiography and cardiac CT. Pitch = table movement per rotation ÷ total beam collimation; pitch > 1 reduces dose and scan time but may reduce image quality.

material.heading: CT numbers and parameters
material.body: Each pixel represents the attenuation of a voxel, expressed in Hounsfield units (HU): water 0, air −1,000, fat about −100, soft tissue +20 to +80, blood (acute clot) +50 to +80, bone +400 to +1,000 or more. Windowing adjusts display: window width (range of HU displayed — narrow for brain and soft tissue, wide for lung and bone) and window level (centre HU). Scan parameters: kVp, mA and rotation time (mAs), slice thickness, pitch, field of view, and reconstruction kernel (soft tissue vs bone/lung sharp kernels). Image quality factors: spatial resolution, contrast resolution (CT's major advantage over radiography), noise (reduced by higher mAs or thicker slices) and artefacts.
keyPoints: Narrow window: soft tissue; wide: lung/bone

topics.title: CT Artefacts, Dose and Clinical Protocols
topics.summary: Common artefacts, dose descriptors and reduction, and protocols for head, chest and abdomen.

material.heading: Artefacts and dose
material.body: CT artefacts: motion (blurring, streaks — reduce with short scan times, breath-holding, immobilisation), beam hardening (dark streaks between dense objects, e.g. posterior fossa between the petrous bones; 'cupping'), metal streak artefacts (reduced by metal artefact reduction algorithms), partial volume averaging (thin slices reduce it), ring artefacts (detector calibration faults) and photon starvation (noise in wide body parts). CT delivers relatively high doses (e.g. head ~2 mSv, abdomen–pelvis ~8–10 mSv). Dose descriptors: CTDIvol (dose per slice/volume, mGy) and dose–length product (DLP = CTDIvol × scan length, mGy·cm), from which effective dose can be estimated. Dose reduction: justification, automatic tube current modulation, lower kVp for children and CT angiography, iterative reconstruction, limiting scan range and phases, and child-specific protocols.

material.heading: Common protocols
material.body: Non-contrast CT head is the first-line test for acute stroke (to exclude haemorrhage before thrombolysis) and head injury. CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) detects pulmonary embolism with contrast timed to the pulmonary arteries. Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen/pelvis (portal venous phase ~60–70 s) evaluates abdominal pain, trauma, abscesses and cancer staging; multiphase liver imaging (arterial, portal venous and delayed) characterises lesions such as hepatocellular carcinoma. CT KUB (non-contrast, low dose) detects urinary stones. High-resolution CT (thin sections, sharp kernel) assesses interstitial lung disease. Trauma CT ('pan-scan') evaluates multiply injured patients rapidly.

topics.title: MRI Physics
topics.summary: Nuclear magnetism, resonance, relaxation (T1 and T2), and image weighting.

material.heading: Signal generation
material.body: MRI uses the magnetic properties of hydrogen nuclei (protons), abundant in water and fat. In a strong static magnetic field (B0, commonly 1.5 or 3 tesla, produced by superconducting magnets cooled with liquid helium), protons align and precess at the Larmor frequency (ω = γB0; about 42.58 MHz per tesla for hydrogen). A radiofrequency (RF) pulse at the Larmor frequency tips the net magnetisation (resonance); after the pulse, protons relax and emit a signal detected by receiver coils. Gradient coils vary the field spatially to encode position (slice selection, frequency and phase encoding), producing the loud knocking noise; data fill k-space, which is converted into an image by Fourier transformation.

material.heading: Relaxation and weighting
material.body: T1 (longitudinal, spin–lattice) relaxation is the recovery of longitudinal magnetisation; T2 (transverse, spin–spin) relaxation is the decay of transverse magnetisation. Fat has short T1 (bright on T1-weighted images); water/CSF has long T1 (dark on T1) and long T2 (bright on T2). T1-weighted images (short TR, short TE) show anatomy well and gadolinium enhancement; T2-weighted images (long TR, long TE) show fluid, oedema and most pathology as bright. Proton density images use long TR and short TE. FLAIR (fluid-attenuated inversion recovery) suppresses CSF signal to reveal periventricular lesions (e.g. multiple sclerosis); STIR suppresses fat. Diffusion-weighted imaging detects acute ischaemic stroke within minutes (restricted diffusion — bright on DWI, dark on ADC map).
keyPoints: T1: short TR/TE; T2: long TR/TE
FLAIR suppresses CSF; STIR suppresses fat

topics.title: MRI Safety
topics.summary: Static field, gradient and RF hazards, implants, screening and quench.

material.heading: Hazards
material.body: MRI does not use ionising radiation but has serious hazards. The static magnetic field (always on) attracts ferromagnetic objects with great force — the projectile ('missile') effect (oxygen cylinders, scissors, trolleys) has caused deaths; only MR-safe or MR-conditional equipment enters the scanner room. Implants and devices: cardiac pacemakers and defibrillators (unless MR-conditional and programmed), cochlear implants, some aneurysm clips, neurostimulators, and metallic foreign bodies (especially intra-orbital — screen metalworkers with orbital X-ray). Radiofrequency energy deposits heat (specific absorption rate, SAR) — burns may occur from conductive loops (crossed limbs, cables touching skin) and tattoos. Rapidly switching gradients cause peripheral nerve stimulation and loud noise (hearing protection required).

material.heading: Safety systems
material.body: MRI units are organised into safety zones (I–IV), with Zone IV being the scanner room, access restricted and controlled by MR-trained staff. Every person (patients, relatives, staff) must complete a screening questionnaire before entering. Pregnant patients may be scanned when clinically indicated (preferably avoiding the first trimester and gadolinium). In a medical emergency, the patient should be removed from Zone IV before resuscitation with standard equipment. A quench is the rapid boiling-off of liquid helium to switch off the superconducting magnet — used only in emergencies (e.g. a person pinned by an object); the vent must carry helium outside, since escaped helium can cause asphyxia and cold burns. Claustrophobia may require reassurance, open or wide-bore scanners or sedation.
keyPoints: Zones I–IV; Zone IV = scanner room
Remove patient from Zone IV for resuscitation

topics.title: Contrast Agents in CT and MRI
topics.summary: Iodinated and gadolinium contrast, reactions, renal considerations and management.

material.heading: Iodinated contrast
material.body: Iodinated contrast media increase X-ray attenuation (iodine's K-edge at 33 keV matches diagnostic energies). Modern agents are low-osmolar or iso-osmolar non-ionic media (e.g. iohexol, iodixanol), safer than older high-osmolar ionic agents. Adverse reactions: mild (warmth, nausea, urticaria), moderate (bronchospasm, facial oedema) and severe (anaphylactoid shock, laryngeal oedema, cardiac arrest) — rare with modern agents; risk factors include previous reaction, asthma and multiple allergies. Management: stop the injection, assess ABC, IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (1:1000) for anaphylaxis, oxygen, IV fluids, antihistamines and steroids. Post-contrast acute kidney injury risk is higher in patients with reduced eGFR (e.g. < 30), diabetes and dehydration — check renal function and hydrate. Metformin may be withheld after contrast in patients with significant renal impairment. Extravasation is managed by elevation and cold compresses.

material.heading: Gadolinium
material.body: Gadolinium-based contrast agents shorten T1, making enhancing tissues bright on T1-weighted images (tumours, inflammation, breakdown of the blood–brain barrier, angiography). Gadolinium is chelated because free gadolinium is toxic. Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis — a rare, serious fibrosing condition — occurs in patients with severe renal impairment given linear, less stable agents; macrocyclic agents are preferred and doses minimised. Gadolinium deposits in the brain have been observed after repeated doses (clinical significance uncertain). Gadolinium is generally avoided in pregnancy unless essential. Allergic reactions are less common than with iodinated agents.
